newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to cut armed forces, but need more weapons.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to cut armed forces, but need more weapons.

text.p: Military experts welcome Taiwan's plan to trim its armed forces, but say the island will need more advanced weapons to fortify itself against its giant neighbour and arch rival -- China.
Taiwan's Defence Ministry gave details of its military reduction plan last week, saying it would cut the number of armed forces personnel from 453,000 to 400,000 over four years.
The Nationalist government says 400,000 troops are sufficient to defend Taiwan's 21 million people because the island no longer seeks to reconquer the mainland.
The Nationalists lost a civil war to China's communists in 1949 and fled to Taiwan. China considers Taiwan as a renegade province and vows to retake it some day, by force if necessary.

"In terms of the number of people in the military, we are always incomparable -- communist China has three million military people and we only have about 450,000," military expert Andrew Yang told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"The cut from 450,000 to 400,000 is not a major reduction. But it will help improve efficiency and modernisation," he said.
Experts said Taiwan also needed to beef up its air defences and quickly install a sophisticated anti-missile system, such as the Patriot missiles it bought from the United States.
Taiwan has already bought fighter planes, missiles and naval vessels to counter the mainland's large military force just across the Taiwan Strait.

Analysts say future purchases could become harder because of Taiwan's diplomatic isolation -- it has formal ties with only 30 countries, mostly underdeveloped nations in Africa and Latin America -- and the view that the island is already well armed.

"The unfavourable political environment makes our arms purchases very difficult," Yang said, referring to the diplomatic isolation imposed by China and Beijing's vehement opposition to foreign arms sales to the island.
Beijing views the establishment of military links with Taiwan and sales of advanced foreign military technology as an encroachment on its sovereignty.
Taiwan has ordered 60 Mirage 2000-5 and 150 F-16 fighters, saying it needs the French and U.S.-made aircraft to counter the steady modernisation of China's People's Liberalisation Army.

China put its military clout on display during war games and missile tests near Taiwan in 1995 and 1996, saying they were intended to cool any ideas of establishing an independent Taiwan in the run-up to the island's first direct presidential election in March 1996.
The United States in 1996 also agreed to sell Taiwan 1,299 Stinger missiles, launchers and 74 Avenger fire units.

It has also approved the sale of 54 AGM-84A Harpoon missiles and 21 Super Cobra attack helicopters, local media has reported. Taiwan's government, under its practise of maintaining silence on defence purchases, would not confirm the deal.
The navy has also taken delivery of two of the six Lafayette-class missile frigates ordered from France.
In March, Taiwan said its deal to buy shoulder-fired Mistral missiles from France had collapsed but would not comment on reports that pressure from China was to blame.
But Yang said further purchases would be more difficult. "Other countries will think Taiwan can maintain the so-called military balance for at least 10 years or so now."

Taiwan's cabinet has proposed a 3.1 percent rise to T$260.2 billion (US$9.5 billion) in defence spending for the 1997/98 (July/June) financial year, representing a fifth of the total budget of T$1.2435 trillion ($45.22 billion).
Also, it proposed a special T$47.4 billion ($1.7 billion) budget to buy French and U.S. warplanes, part of a nine-year T$300.7 billion ($11 billion) fighter procurement fund.
